Fashion has the highest return rate of any sector, and usually one cause: size. And the customer here is not buying a piece, she is buying a look - an abaya alone is not a look; the scarf and the bag are what complete it. So the moments below serve two goals at once: raising the basket, and cutting the returns that eat the margin on the basket you just raised.
The whole look, not the single piece
The customer adds an abaya to the cart.
The scarf and the bag appear exactly as styled in the product photo itself, not as separate products. She liked the whole image, so sell her the image.
The product photo is the advert. Offering exactly the pieces in it turns liking the image into an order, whereas "related products" sends her back to browsing.
A 450 abaya → "The scarf and bag from the same photo, 220 for both".
The right size before the order
The customer hesitates between two sizes.
The garment's real measurements in centimetres appear, compared with what she bought before: "Runs one size smaller than the abaya you ordered in March".
A size return costs two shipments and the entire margin on the piece. Her purchase history knows her real size better than any size chart.
Hesitating between M and L → "You ordered M in March; this runs smaller - take the L".
L - this one runs a size small
The customer browses in a hot or a cold season.
Season-appropriate fabrics move up the ranking: light crepe in summer, lined in winter. A beautiful piece in the wrong season comes back.
Seasonal ranking lifts conversion and cuts returns at the same time. A customer receiving a heavy abaya in July will not wear it however much she liked it.
Browsing in July → light crepe first, lined pieces at the end of the page.
The same design in a second colour
The customer bought a piece before and returns to the same design.
The second colour of the same design is offered at a reduced price for the second piece. The fit is already proven, so the risk is zero and returns are near nil.
The highest basket in fashion and the lowest return rate are the same thing: a design she has tried and that worked. Repeating it in another colour is margin with no risk.
A black abaya bought and fitting well → "The same cut in navy, 20% off the second".
Closing the shipping gap with an accessory, not a second garment
The cart is close to the free-shipping threshold.
A small accessory closes the gap - a scarf, a belt, a brooch - rather than a second abaya worth twice the gap. Accessories are almost never returned.
Pushing a second large garment to close a shipping gap raises the basket today and raises returns next week, which nets out negative.
Cart at 380, free shipping at 400 → a 45 SAR scarf, not a 390 SAR abaya.
The customer opens a piece and her size is out of stock.
An alert for her size specifically is offered, along with two close pieces available in her size right now. She is never left at a dead end.
A dead-end page ends the visit. Turning it into two available options plus a later alert keeps both the visit and the customer.
M out of stock → "Notify me" + two pieces in the same cut available in M.

Skincare sells by routine, not by item. A serum has a step before it and a step after it, and a customer who buys one step and skips the next blames the product when it underdelivers. And every bottle has a known life: a serum runs out in six weeks, a sunscreen in eight. Those two facts - the routine and the shelf life - are what Ziadah builds on here, not generic "related products".
The next step in the routine
The customer adds a vitamin C serum to the cart.
A moisturiser and a sunscreen appear as the next two steps, with a reason rather than a push: "Vitamin C needs sunscreen after it, or its effect is wasted".

This is not an upsell, it is rescuing the first product. A customer using vitamin C without sunscreen sees no result and does not reorder, so the suggestion protects the repeat purchase, not just this order.
Vitamin C serum → a light moisturiser + SPF 50 sunscreen. The routine complete in three steps.
Vitamin C needs sunscreen after it
Refill timing: before the bottle runs out
Six weeks have passed since a 30ml serum was bought.
The reorder suggestion arrives days before it runs out rather than weeks after, because one week off the routine breaks the habit and she may not come back.
Most beauty stores lose the customer in the gap between running out and remembering to reorder. Bottle size and usage rate are both known, so the timing is arithmetic rather than a guess.
A 30ml serum bought on 1 March → a reminder on 8 April, with an offer on the larger size.
Matching by skin type, not by category
The customer has browsed three products for oily skin.
Later suggestions are filtered by the skin type inferred from behaviour, so a heavy cream is never shown for oily skin even if it is the store's bestseller.
A wrong suggestion hurts more here than anywhere else: a product that does not suit the skin does visible damage, and the customer blames the store rather than herself.
Behaviour indicating oily skin → a water gel instead of the rich cream, even though the cream outsells it.
Filtered to oily skin from your browsing
The matching shade, not a random one
The customer adds a foundation in a specific shade.

Concealer and powder are suggested in the shade that matches what she actually picked, not the best-selling shade. Shade choice is the hardest decision in online make-up and the biggest cause of returns.
Every return over a wrong shade costs shipping twice and trust once. Matching correctly raises the order and lowers returns at the same time.
Foundation in 320 → concealer in 320 and a translucent powder, not the top-selling shade.
In your shade, not the bestseller
From the sample to the full size
The customer bought a travel size or a sample weeks ago.
After enough time to have tried it, the full size appears with the unit-price difference spelled out: "The full size saves 40% per ml".
A sample is a sales tool, not a product. A store that does not follow it with the full size at the right moment has paid for the trial and left the margin.
A 15ml sample at 45 → the 50ml at 120 (40% less per ml).
The whole routine at a bundle price
The cart holds two steps of a three-step routine.
"One toner away from the complete night routine, 45 less" - it names the missing step, so she is not hunting through a hundred products for the right one.
Selling the whole routine raises the order and raises the result she actually sees, which is the only thing that brings her back. The bundle here is a prescription, not a discount.
Cleanser + serum in the cart → "Add the toner: the full routine at 260 instead of 305".
Closing the free-shipping gap with small items
The cart is a small amount below the free-shipping threshold.
Small items that close the gap exactly are suggested - a sheet mask, a travel size, a brush - not a product worth twice the gap.
Beauty is full of small high-margin items, which are exactly what closes a shipping gap without the suggestion reading as a squeeze.
Cart at 165, free shipping at 200 → two sheet masks at 15, or a travel size at 35.
Gifting: a different season, different rules
The order falls in a gifting season, or gift wrapping is selected.
The suggestions change entirely: ready gift sets and fragrance rise above routine products, because a gift buyer does not know the recipient's skin type and will not risk it.

A gift buyer shops on the opposite logic to someone buying for herself: they want safety and presentation, not suitability. Suggesting a specialist serum as a gift is a wrong suggestion however good the serum is.
Gift wrapping on → a ready 320 SAR care set, not a specialist sensitive-skin serum.

A charity has no margin, no basket and no customer. It has a donor, and only two numbers matter: whether they give again, and whether they move to monthly. So "raising order value" here means turning a single gift into a recurring one, and every moment below is written to respect a donor rather than convert a shopper - no manufactured urgency, no guilt, no inflated impact claims. A charity that pushes too hard loses the donor for life, not just this gift.
The donor completes a one-off gift.
After the thank-you, never before it, the same amount is offered as monthly with its cumulative effect: "200 a month covers a student for a full year". Same figure, different horizon.
A monthly donor is worth many times an occasional one, and the only moment they are open to committing is right after a gift they have just made and feel good about.
A 200 SAR gift → "Make it monthly: 200 × 12 covers one student for a year".
Completing a project that is nearly there
The donor is viewing a project that has reached 90% of its goal.
The exact remaining amount is shown: "400 SAR left and the well is complete". A gift that finishes something lands differently from a gift added to an open fund.
"I finished something" is a different feeling from "I contributed to a fund". A specific figure and a visible finish line are what turn browsing into giving.
A well at 11,600 of 12,000 → "Finish it with 400 SAR".
The donor visits during Ramadan or near their zakat due date.
Zakat-eligible projects come first, and the zakat calculator appears before the project list. A donor in Ramadan is looking for the right channel, not for persuasion.
Most of the year's giving happens in one month. A charity that shows the same ordering in Ramadan as in March wastes the season that funds it.
A Ramadan visit → the zakat calculator first, then eligible projects ordered by how close they are to completion.
What your last gift did, before asking for the next
Enough time has passed on a previous gift for its effect to be visible.
An impact message arrives first with no ask in it at all: "Your well has been running three months, serving 40 families". The next ask comes in a separate message later.
A charity that never tells a donor what happened is asking them to trust twice. Showing the effect first is what makes the second ask welcome.
A well funded in January → April: "Your well is running, 40 families", with no ask attached.
The amount ladder, by effect rather than by figure
The donor is on the amount screen.

Every amount is written as what it does rather than as a figure alone: "100 = a food basket for a family, 300 = three families, 500 = one family for a whole month". The ladder starts from the middle, not the top.

A bare figure is compared against a budget; a figure translated into effect is compared against the effect. And leading with the highest amount reads as pressure and lowers the average rather than raising it.
100 one basket · 300 three families · 500 a family for a month - with 300 preselected.
Every amount by what it does
A monthly charge fails, or the card expires.
A calm operational message with no blame: "Your card expired, the monthly gift is paused", and one link to update it. No guilt, no reminder of what was lost.
Most lapsed monthly giving is technical, not a decision. Treating it as a decision, with emotional messaging, turns a card problem into a real withdrawal.
A failed charge on 1 May → one blame-free message and a link to update the card.
A project in the same cause, not from all of them
The donor has previously given to education projects.
Education projects come first, not everything the charity runs. A donor picks a cause rather than an organisation, and suggesting a different one reads as nobody having noticed what they chose.
Every donor has a cause they return to. Respecting that choice lifts second-gift rates more than any rewording of the ask.
A previous student sponsorship → education projects first. Not relief, not mosques.
It is an occasion season, or the donor chooses to dedicate the gift.
A "on behalf of" option with a card sent to the recipient or their family. An entirely different kind of gift: its occasion is a social one, not a campaign.
Giving on behalf of parents or of someone who has passed is a deeply established pattern here, and a channel that adds to the others rather than competing with them.
"An ongoing charity on behalf of my father" → a card in his name sent to the family.

A clinic does not sell a product, it books time. The unit is an appointment, the constraint is a calendar rather than stock, and the sector is regulated: no suggestion may read as medical advice or promise an outcome. So every moment below suggests a session, a package, preparation or follow-up - never a diagnosis, and never a procedure the patient did not ask about themselves.
The package instead of the single session
The patient books a single session of a procedure that normally needs a series.
The package appears with its session count and the per-session price inside it: "6 sessions - 320 each instead of 450". No outcome promised, just the arithmetic.

A patient booking one session of a series will either book the rest anyway or drop out. The package locks in the commitment and fills the calendar in advance, which is the number a clinic's economics turn on.
One laser session at 450 → a 6-session package at 1920 (320 each).
The session is done and the procedure has known aftercare requirements.
The clinic's own approved aftercare appears - a medical sunscreen, a calming moisturiser - framed as part of the instructions rather than as an offer.
Aftercare genuinely determines the result, and a patient who buys it from a random pharmacy may buy the wrong thing. Selling it here serves the outcome before it serves the bill.
After a peel → a 180 SAR medical sunscreen and a 140 SAR calming moisturiser, inside the discharge instructions.
The session ends and the protocol calls for follow-up after a known interval.
The follow-up is offered with its date while they are still in the clinic, not in a message a month later. Booking while they are present is ten times easier than winning them back.
The gap between a session and its follow-up is where clinics lose patients. Closing it does not need a marketing campaign, just a suggestion at the right moment.
Today's session → "Follow-up in 4 weeks: Tuesday the 14th at 6pm", in one tap.
A booking is made for a procedure with preparation requirements.

Preparation instructions arrive with enough lead time, with anything that needs buying alongside them. An appointment cancelled for lack of preparation is a double loss: a hole in the calendar and a frustrated patient.
Last-minute cancellation is the most expensive operational problem a clinic has, and its commonest cause is the simplest: the patient did not know what to do beforehand.
A Thursday booking → a Tuesday reminder with the preparation steps and anything to buy first.
The complementary service in the same visit
The patient books a service that commonly pairs with another.
Adding the paired service to the same visit is offered with the time saving stated: "In the same appointment, 20 minutes more". Time is a stronger argument here than price.
Every extra visit costs the patient travel and time off work. Combining two services in one visit raises the value of the appointment and lowers their burden at once.
A dental cleaning → "Whitening in the same appointment, 40 minutes more" instead of a second visit.
The usual interval between check-ups has passed since the patient's last visit.
A neutral reminder: "Six months since your last cleaning" - a fact rather than advice, and the decision stays with the patient.
The clinic knows the date of the last visit and nobody else does. Turning that into a timely reminder is the cheapest source of appointments any clinic has.
Last cleaning in March → a September reminder with the next three open slots.
The family's appointments in one visit
A patient books for themselves and has family members on file.
Back-to-back slots for family members in the same window are offered, turning three visits into one. Shown only for members already on file, and only with prior consent.
Families already coordinate their visits, and a clinic that does not make that easy pushes them to split between two clinics.
Father booked Thursday 5pm → "The children at 5:30 and 6 in the same visit?"
An appointment is cancelled or missed.
The freed slot is offered immediately to the waiting list for that service, and the person who cancelled is offered the nearest alternative. The hole is filled in minutes instead of being lost.
An empty hour in a clinic calendar is a full unrecoverable cost: the staff are there and the rent is running. Filling the hole matters more than selling anything extra.
A 4pm cancellation → offered instantly to that service's waiting list, with an alternative pushed to the person who cancelled.

A delivery app is a marketplace, not a store: the user opens it hungry without knowing what they want, and closes it if they cannot decide in two minutes. The moments below are written for that economics specifically.
Minimum order: how far you are from it
The basket is under the restaurant's minimum.
The gap in riyals with two items that close it exactly, sorted by smallest overshoot. A user who sees "9 SAR short" and no way to close it abandons the basket.
Abandonment at the minimum is the biggest leak in delivery apps, and the cause is informational rather than price: the user does not know what to add.
Basket at 41, minimum 50 → "cookies 8" or "a drink 9", not a 35 SAR dish.
The order is confirmed and the rider is on the way.
During tracking, one item can be added as a linked order from the same kitchen before it leaves. The tracking minutes are time the user already spends staring at the screen.
This is the one window where a suggestion competes with nothing: no queue, no browsing, no other open decision.
Order leaving the kitchen in 8 minutes → "Add a dessert before it goes".
A repeat user opens the app at their usual hour.
The usual order sits at the top in one tap, with one item from the same restaurant they have never tried.
A user who decides fast orders more often. Shortening the decision lifts frequency, and the single new item widens the basket without slowing them down.
9pm Thursday → "The usual: shawarma and a Pepsi" + "Try the cheese fries".
Group ordering: a basket that multiplies
The order falls in a work-lunch or family-gathering window.
Family sizes and platters are suggested instead of single plates, with a link that shares the basket so each person adds their own.
A group order is the highest basket in the app and the lowest delivery cost per riyal. Making it technically easy doubles the value with no discount at all.
12:30pm from an office location → "A 6-person platter" + a basket-sharing link.
Discovery: a nearby place they have not tried
The user has browsed without ordering for more than two minutes.
One nearby restaurant similar to what they usually order, with its delivery time and rating. One suggestion, not a list - the list is the problem in the first place.
Long browsing without ordering signals choice paralysis rather than disinterest. Narrowing to one is the fix; widening makes it worse.
3 minutes browsing with no order → "Al-Dana Grills, 25 minutes, 4.7" - one suggestion.
The restaurant is at peak and preparation time has risen.
Fast-prep items move up the ranking and slow ones move down. The suggestion here serves delivery time rather than basket value.
Ratings in delivery apps follow time rather than taste. Suggesting a slow item at peak earns a riyal and loses a star.
8:30pm with a busy kitchen → sandwiches are suggested, not grills.

Digital cards are a speed business: the customer arrives knowing exactly what they want and wants the code within a second. Margin is very thin and competing on price is near impossible, so the profit comes from the higher denomination and from repeat purchase, not from raising the price. Any friction loses the order instantly, because the alternative is one search away.
The higher denomination for a small difference
The customer picks a mid denomination.
The higher denomination appears with its difference and its meaning: "100 instead of 50 covers two months instead of one". The benefit stated in time, not in figures.
The higher denomination means one visit instead of two and one processing fee instead of two. Both sides gain.
A 50 card → "100 covers two months, and you pay the processing fee once".
And one processing fee instead of two
The companion card for the same player
The customer buys a gaming platform card.
The companion subscription for the same platform is offered, not for a different one: the online membership alongside the store credit.
A gamer is locked to one platform. Suggesting a rival platform's card proves the store does not know them, which is the fastest way to lose the repeat.
Game store credit → "12-month online membership" for the same platform.
The customer is comparing your store with another.
Delivery time is stated beside the price: "Code in 30 seconds". In a sector where price competition is impossible, speed is the product.
Someone buying a card is buying it because they want it now. A store a riyal cheaper that delivers in an hour loses to one that delivers instantly.
A card page → "Delivered in 30 seconds" beside the price, not at the bottom.
The customer buys the same card roughly monthly.
A reminder a day before it is due, with the code one tap away. They will buy it anyway; the only question is from where.
There is no loyalty in this sector, only habit. Whoever reminds first owns the habit, and a day late loses it.
Bought on the 1st each month → a reminder on the 30th with the code ready.
The order falls in a gift season, or the customer picks a large denomination.
Sending the code straight to the recipient with a message is offered, instead of receiving it and forwarding it by hand.
A digital card is a common gift and an awkward one to present: forwarding a bare code reads as cold. Wrapping it digitally adds value at no cost.
A 200 card → "Send it straight to their number with your message" instead of receiving it.
Send to their number with your message

A digital product has zero marginal cost: the second copy costs nothing, and there is no stock, no shipping and no size. That inverts the economics - a bundle here is not a margin concession, it is pure additional margin. And the real problem is not selling but using: whoever buys a course and never opens it does not buy the second one.
The bundle that costs nothing to make
The customer adds a single digital product.
A three-product bundle appears at less than the sum of its parts. There is no added cost to the store at all, so every riyal in the difference is margin.
With physical goods a bundle concedes margin. Here it is entirely incremental, and yet most digital stores price as though they were selling shirts.
One template at 120 → "The full pack, 8 templates for 390 instead of 960".
Days have passed since purchase with no download or login.
A message that helps them start rather than buy: the first step, the shortest video, the starter file. No new offer at all.
Someone who never used what they bought will not buy again and will ask for a refund. Usage is the precondition for the second purchase, and nothing else is.
A course bought 5 days ago with no login → "Start with lesson one, 7 minutes".
The upgrade after they hit the limit
The user approaches their plan's limit.
The upgrade is offered at 80% of the limit rather than at signup: "8 of your 10 projects used". The need has proved itself before the offer.
Offering the higher plan before they touch the limit reads as greed. Offering it as they are about to hit it reads as a useful heads-up.
8 of 10 projects used → "The higher plan: unlimited projects, +40 a month".
The add-on on the thank-you page
Payment is done and the download page appears.
One offer on the download page: a complementary add-on at a one-time price. The card is already out and the friction is at its lowest.
The moment after payment is the highest-acceptance point in the whole funnel and costs nothing. But one offer only - a second one ruins the trust just earned.
After buying a template → "The editable source files, 65 SAR one time".
The commercial licence for commercial use
The customer buys an asset that has two licence tiers.
The difference is explained by use rather than by name: "Personal: your own projects. Commercial: your clients' projects". No legal jargon.
Most people who buy the personal licence and use it commercially are not cheating, they misread it. Explaining by use sells the higher tier and protects your rights at once.
A 120 personal template → "Commercial at 290: use it in your clients' work".
The new version for whoever bought the old one
A new version ships of a product the customer owns.
The new version is offered at an upgrade price rather than the full one. An existing owner is the easiest customer on the list and the cheapest to reach.
The existing customer base is the real asset in digital products. Selling the new version to it with zero acquisition cost is the highest margin available.
Bought version 2 → "Version 3 at an upgrade price of 45 instead of 120".

A multi-vendor marketplace has the opposite problem to a store: not too little supply but far too much. The buyer drowns in thousands of products from hundreds of sellers, and the platform earns a commission per order rather than a margin per product. So the goal here is not lifting one basket - it is shortening the path to a decision, and distributing visibility fairly across sellers so the platform does not lose its supply side.
Narrowing the options, not widening them
The buyer has browsed a long time without adding to cart.
Three products with clear differences between them, not forty results. Long browsing is choice paralysis, and showing more makes it worse.
Recommendation on a marketplace does the opposite job to recommendation in a store: a store widens discovery, a marketplace closes a decision.
6 minutes browsing with nothing added → 3 options: cheapest, best rated, fastest to arrive.
Consolidating the order with one seller
The cart holds an item from a seller with other suitable products.
Products from the same seller are offered to save shipping: "Add from the same seller, one shipment". Both sides' interests align here.
An order split across three sellers means three shipments, three chances of delay and three chances of a bad rating. Consolidating raises the basket and lowers the risk.
An item from seller A → "Two more from the same seller: one shipment, 25 saved".
Several sellers offer an equivalent product.
Visibility rotates among equivalent sellers instead of pinning the largest one permanently, weighted by rating and delivery time.
A marketplace where one seller always appears loses the others, and losing the supply side kills a marketplace faster than losing the demand side.
5 sellers of the same item → rotation weighted by rating rather than by seller size.
Ranked by rating, not seller size
The buyer completes an order in one category.
A product from an adjacent category that this type of buyer also purchases is shown. A buyer active in one category assumes the marketplace only does that category.
The most important number on a marketplace is how many categories a single user buys from. Each extra category multiplies their lifetime value.
Completed an electronics order → "Electronics buyers also buy this from Office".
A desk organiser - electronics buyers buy this
Delivery certainty as a ranking signal
The buyer compares offers at similar prices.
The offer with the highest delivery certainty ranks above the one a riyal cheaper. "Arrives tomorrow" closes better than "two riyals less".
A marketplace is judged on delivery, not on price. Ranking on price alone wins an order today and loses a user after one late arrival.
Two offers 3 SAR apart → "Arrives tomorrow" outranks "Arrives in 5 days".
The new seller with no history
A new seller has listed products with no data behind them.
Their products get a measured share of visibility early, instead of waiting for data that cannot arrive without visibility. A loop broken by a decision rather than by an algorithm.
An algorithm ranking purely on performance strangles every new seller, so nobody joins. A marketplace needs a flow of sellers more than it needs a perfect ranking.
A new seller → a fixed share of impressions for 30 days, then ranked on performance.
An item with no sales history
A share of impressions for 30 days

Electronics runs thin margin on the device and fat margin on everything around it: the device's price is compared across ten stores, the accessory is not. And a device without its accessory is genuinely incomplete - an unprotected phone breaks, a monitor without the right cable never reaches its rated resolution. So every moment here is about completing the device rather than selling a second one.
Protection with the device, not after it breaks
A shopper who has just put three to five thousand on a device and is still in the moment of caring about it.
The customer adds a phone or tablet to the cart.
A case and screen protector appear in the exact fit for that model, not as a generic category. The wrong fit is the single biggest cause of accessory returns.
The customer will buy protection within a fortnight anyway - from you or from a kiosk at the traffic lights. Selling it in the same order captures margin that was walking out.
iPhone 15 Pro → a model-matched case at 120 + a screen protector at 85, by fit and not by category.
What the device needs to work at all
A shopper who does not know the box is incomplete, and will not find out until they open it at home.
The customer adds a device that needs a cable or charger not in the box.
The suggestion states the gap outright: "No charger in the box" - and offers the compatible one. This rescues the unboxing rather than adding a sale.
A customer who opens the box and cannot power the device writes a bad review about the store, not the manufacturer. The warning protects the rating before it lifts the basket.
A phone with no charger included → "Needs a 20W charger" + the right cable.
So it works on day one
Storage upgrade by the price difference
A shopper weighing two prices with nothing that turns the gap into a difference in their own life.
The customer is viewing the lowest storage tier of a model.
The difference to the higher tier appears with what it means in practice: "+400 SAR = double the space, roughly 20,000 more photos".
Storage is the one irreversible decision: it cannot be upgraded later. A customer not warned now buys a whole new device in two years over space.
128GB → "256 for 400 more, double the space, and it cannot be upgraded later".
The whole setup at a bundle price
Someone building a desk or a gaming corner who will buy four pieces within the month regardless.
The customer buys one piece of a known setup.
The rest of the setup is offered as a bundle: monitor + keyboard + mouse + stand. Someone building a desk buys all of it, so the question is where rather than whether.
Bundling the setup stops the customer splitting the order across three stores, which is the default when no bundle exists.
A 27-inch monitor → "The full setup at 1850 instead of 2140", stand and cable included.
Extended warranty at the decision, not after it
A high-value buyer who has reached checkout, committed to the purchase and now weighing risk rather than price.
The customer is at checkout for a high-value device.
Extended warranty appears with its price and what it covers in one line. It shows once and never repeats - repeating it reads as fear about the product's quality.
Warranty is the highest-margin line in the order and the lowest operational cost. It is also the fastest way to damage trust if pushed.
A 6,500 laptop → "Two extra years at 450, accidental damage included" - shown once.
Two more years - accidental damage included
A past customer who bought months ago and has forgotten the device has a part that needs replacing.
Time has passed on a device with a consumable of known life.
A reminder to reorder the consumable before it runs out: a filter, ink, a brush head. The customer does not remember the filter schedule; the store does.
Consumables are guaranteed recurring revenue that leaks entirely to the big marketplaces for one reason: they remind and the smaller store does not.
A water filter bought in January with a six-month life → a reminder in June.
What owners of the same device actually bought
A first-time buyer in a category they do not know, with no idea what they will need a week later.
The customer is viewing a device hundreds of customers bought before them.
The three parts most often bought with this exact model appear with the share stated plainly: "68% of people who bought this monitor took the arm mount with it".
In electronics a new buyer does not trust the store's opinion but does trust the behaviour of those before them. The number turns a pitch into information.
A 27-inch monitor → "68% took the arm mount, 41% took a DisplayPort cable".
68% of people who bought this monitor
Cables by the pack, not by the piece
A customer buying one cable while owning three devices that take the same cable.
The customer adds a cheap, losable, repeat item: a cable, a charger, a battery.
A small progressive table appears: one for 45, three for 110, five for 165. No pressure and no timer - the table is enough because the logic is visible.
A cable gets lost, frayed, left at the office. Whoever buys one comes back in two months, usually to another store. Selling three now buys two months of not coming back.
A USB-C cable at 45 → "3 for 110 (save 25), 5 for 165 (save 60)".
The more you take, the less each one costs
Closing the shipping gap with something useful
A customer sitting just under the free-shipping threshold, watching the delivery fee being added.
The cart is under the free-shipping threshold by less than 100 SAR.
The exact gap appears alongside two items priced to cover it that the customer will genuinely use: "58 SAR away from free delivery".
The customer pays 30 in delivery or adds 58 in goods. The second is better for both sides, but only happens if they know the gap and can see what closes it.
A 142 cart against a 200 threshold → "58 to go" + a phone stand at 65 or a cable case at 60.
Add either one and the delivery fee goes
The coupon on the way out, not before
A customer who has price-checked the device elsewhere and is heading out to buy it there.
Exit signals on a cart holding a price-compared device.
A time-boxed coupon appears for this cart specifically, worth less than the device's margin and more than the usual price gap in the market.
In electronics the gap between two stores is usually 2% to 4%. A 5% coupon ends the comparison, and it is far cheaper than losing the whole order with its accessories.
A 5,200 cart at exit → "5% off for 15 minutes on this cart".
The better alternative while comparing, not after deciding
A browser on a category page with five models open in tabs and nothing decided.
The customer is browsing a category and lands on a lower-tier model.
The higher model appears with a single difference line: what it adds, and what it costs more. Not a ten-row comparison table - one row is what gets read.
On the category page the customer is still comparing, so an upgrade is welcome. Once inside the product page they have chosen, and an upgrade reads as a sales push.
A 320 headphone → "For 180 more: active noise cancelling and double the battery".
The higher model in the same category
The gaming corner as a bundle, not as parts
A console buyer, or a parent buying a gift with no idea what the console is missing.
The customer is in the gaming category or has added a console to the cart.
A ready bundle appears: a second controller + a game + a subscription. Named for what it means - "two can play on day one" - not as a parts list.
A console with one controller is an incomplete experience the buyer discovers in the first session. The bundle sells an outcome, which is easier than arguing for three separate parts.
A console → "Two can play on day one: second controller + a game + 3-month subscription, 790 instead of 930".
Two can play on day one
Memory cards by the pack for people who shoot
A photographer or creator buying one card today who will need three before the season ends.
The customer adds a memory card or an external drive to the cart.
The per-unit price at each quantity appears with the reason: "a spare in the bag" - not just a discount, but a working habit everyone in this field knows.
Anyone who shoots knows a card fills up or fails at the worst moment. The quantity offer here is not persuading an extra purchase, it is agreeing with a habit that already exists.
A 128GB card at 140 → "2 for 250, 3 for 345 (115 each)".
The per-card price drops with quantity
A customer who knows the part's name and searches for it directly - the highest intent in the store.
The customer searched for a part that does not work on its own.
Alongside the results sits the complementary part half the buyers ask about two days later: a graphics card → a sufficient power supply, a router → a long network cable.
Someone searching an exact part name has decided to buy but usually does not know the hidden requirement. Showing it in the results prevents a return or a support ticket.
A search for "4070 graphics card" → "Needs at least a 750W power supply" with the compatible one.
It will not run on a smaller unit
Rescuing the cart when the expensive line is removed
A customer who has backed out of the most expensive line in their cart, usually over price rather than desire.
The customer removes the priciest product from the cart but has not left.
Two alternatives appear rather than a straight discount: the same part a tier down, or the same part refurbished with warranty. The discount is the last option, not the first.
Removing the expensive line is a budget signal, not a rejection. Offer a discount immediately and the customer learns to wait for one; offer an alternative and they buy today.
A 6,500 laptop removed → "The same model with less memory at 5,200" or "Refurbished with a year's warranty at 4,700".
There are alternatives before you cancel
The same model on a smaller budget

Gold is a commodity and its price is not the store's decision: the gram moves daily and the margin sits in the making charge, not the metal. And the buyer here is two people, not one: an occasion buyer who cares about the design, and a saver who cares about the weight. The moments below separate them, because a suggestion that suits the first insults the second.
Locking the price while they hesitate
The customer is viewing a piece while the gram price moves.
Today's price is shown with how long it holds, stated plainly: "This price holds until 6pm". The transparency here is not pressure, it is how the market works.
A customer who comes back tomorrow to an unexplained different price loses trust. Stating the pricing mechanism up front protects that trust and resolves the hesitation at the same time.
Weight or design: which buyer is this
Browsing behaviour leans towards weight or towards design.
A buyer comparing weights is shown bars and low-making-charge pieces. A buyer comparing designs is shown sets and handcrafted work.

Showing an ornate high-making-charge design to a saver reads as an attempt to take advantage. Showing a bar to someone buying for a wedding reads as not listening. The difference between those two sales is the whole sector.
Compared three pieces by weight → bars and the lowest making charges, not stone-set suites.
The bridal set as a whole, not piece by piece
The customer is viewing one of the usual bridal pieces.
The full set appears with its total weight and a combined making charge, in one image with all the pieces. Buying a bridal set is one decision, not four.
Whoever buys a bridal set buys all of it anyway, and splitting it across four visits opens the door to a competitor's gram price in between.
A bridal ring → "The full set, 85 grams, one combined making charge", in a single image.
The occasions gold is bought for
A wedding, newborn or Eid season approaches.
Occasion-appropriate pieces move up: light newborn bangles, small Eid gifts, bridal pieces in wedding season.
Gold here is bought for a specific occasion rather than at random. Ordering the catalogue by season multiplies relevance with no discount at all.
Newborn season → light 5-8 gram bangles at the front.
The customer is comparing pieces above their apparent budget.
Trading in old gold against the price is offered: "Bring your old pieces and we deduct the weight". It turns a piece that looked out of reach into a close one.
Every household here has old gold nobody wears. Reminding the customer that it is credit rather than jewellery is what opens the budget.
A 12,000 piece out of budget → "Trade in 30 grams of old gold and the difference drops by 11,000".
The certificate and hallmark as part of the offer
The customer is on a high-value piece.
The certificate, the hallmark and the buy-back policy sit beside the price rather than on a separate page. The buyer wants assurance they can sell it again later.
Gold is bought with resale in mind. A store that spells out its buy-back outsells a cheaper store that does not.
A 9,500 piece → "21k hallmark, certificate, buy-back at the day's price less the making charge".
Certificate + buy-back at the day's price

Supplements and equipment are bought for a goal, not for themselves: losing weight, building muscle, endurance. The customer knows the goal and not what it takes, so they buy one item and stop when they see no result. And a supplement has a life measured in servings, so reorder timing is arithmetic rather than a guess. The sector is regulated too: no promised outcomes, no therapeutic claims.
What completes the goal, not what resembles the product
The customer adds whey protein to the cart.
Supplements serving the same goal appear, not the same category: creatine and a shaker, rather than a second flavour of the same protein.
The customer does not want protein, they want muscle. A suggestion that understands the goal sells three items; one that understands the category offers another flavour and sells nothing.
Whey protein → creatine at 120 + a shaker at 45, not the vanilla version of the same tub.
Muscle building - not a second flavour
Running out by servings, not by calendar
A 30-serving tub was bought 26 days ago.
The reminder arrives days before it runs out, computed from the serving count and the stated usage rate. A week's gap breaks the programme and the habit together.
A customer who runs out and cannot reorder instantly buys from the nearest store, not yours. The reminder race is the retention race.
A 30-serving tub, one a day, bought 1 March → a reminder on 27 March.
The bigger tub, priced per serving
The customer buys the same product for a third time.
The larger size is priced per serving rather than per tub: "6.5 a serving instead of 9.2". A third-time buyer has proved they will get through it.
Offering the big tub to a first-time buyer is a gamble; offering it to a third-time buyer is a service. Timing is the whole difference.
A third 1kg purchase → "2.5kg, 6.5 per serving instead of 9.2".
What the equipment needs to be usable
The customer adds weights or a home machine.
A mat, a rack and grip gloves appear - not a second machine. Weights without a mat wreck the floor and end up in storage.
Equipment that goes unused is never repeated and never recommended. Selling what makes it usable at home protects the rating and the referral.
A 20kg weight set → a floor mat at 180 and a rack at 240, not another machine.
To actually use it at home
A new customer with no purchase history in the sector.
Two items in small sizes, not a full supplement stack. A beginner loaded with six products abandons the cart or abandons the programme.
The goal in this sector is not the biggest first order, it is a second order at all. Overselling a beginner kills the repeat, which is where all the margin is.
A new customer → a 1kg protein and a shaker only. No creatine, no burner, no vitamins.
Two items only, not a stack
A monthly subscription instead of a repeated order
The customer has ordered the same items three times at regular intervals.
Turning the repeated order into a subscription is offered, with a fixed discount and delivery on the same date each month. They are already buying this monthly.
A subscription turns a volatile customer into predictable revenue, and shuts the door on the competitor who reminds them a day before you do.
The same order in January, February and March → "Monthly subscription, 10% off, delivered on the 1st".
The same order 3 times, on a rhythm

Home goods are bought on two opposite patterns: consumables that run out on a rhythm and are reordered without thinking, and furniture bought once every few years after long hesitation. The first lives on a timely reminder, the second on removing doubt about size and colour. Mixing them into one suggestion fails at both.
The customer adds a furniture piece to the cart.
The complementary pieces appear as styled in the room photo itself: the side table, the rug and the lamp that were in the shot.
The customer liked the room, not the sofa. Selling what is in the photo turns that into an order; "related products" sends them back to browsing.
A 2,900 sofa → "The rug and table from the same photo, 1,150 for both".
The size in its place, before buying
The customer hesitates on a large piece.
Dimensions appear plainly with a familiar reference: "15cm wider than a standard doorway". The hesitation here is spatial, not financial.
Returning furniture that will not fit through the door costs two heavy shipments, and is the most expensive return in all of ecommerce.
A 95cm-wide wardrobe → "A standard door is 80cm - measure before ordering".
A household consumable has reached its usual cycle.
A reorder reminder sized to the pack and the household: detergents, bags, filters. The customer does not remember until it runs out, and then buys from the corner shop.
Household consumables are guaranteed recurring revenue, and a store that does not remind hands it to the nearest shelf however much dearer it is.
A 5-litre detergent for a household of five, bought 1 March → a reminder on 20 April.
For a household of 5, about 7 weeks
The customer buys a high-consumption item.
The larger count is priced per unit: "6 for 110 instead of 6 × 22". Household consumables do not spoil and need no special storage.
Buying in quantity cuts shipments for the store and cuts decisions for the customer. Both sides win, which is rare.
Hand soap at 22 each → "6 for 110, that's 18.3 each".
A season starts that changes what the house needs.
Seasonal items move up: heavy bedding and rugs in winter, fans and grilling gear in summer, hosting supplies in Ramadan.
Household needs here swing hard by season, and a store showing the same ordering all year is selling summer in December.
The start of Ramadan → hosting sets and serving trays at the front.
The customer buys a piece that needs assembling.
Assembly is offered with its price and duration alongside the order. A customer who discovers after delivery that they must assemble it writes a bad review, fairly.
Assembly is high-margin service revenue and also the fastest way to turn a good furniture experience bad when it is left to the customer unannounced.
A wardrobe needing assembly → "Home assembly 180 SAR, 45 minutes", offered with the order.

Jewellery is bought for an occasion, and usually for somebody else. The buyer is anxious: they do not know the size, they do not know whether the taste will land, and the amount is large enough to postpone the decision. So the moments that work best here are not the ones adding a piece - they are the ones removing an anxiety: a guaranteed size, packaging that fits the occasion, and a clear return.
Completing the set, not adding a piece
The customer adds a necklace from a design that has matching earrings and a bracelet.
The full set appears in a single image showing the pieces together, with a set price. Seeing them together is the argument, not the discount.
Jewellery is worn as a set, not as a piece. A customer buying a lone necklace will hunt for matching earrings later, usually somewhere else.
A 1,400 necklace → the full set at 3,200 instead of 3,750, in one image with all three.
Size anxiety: remove it before checkout
The customer hesitates on a ring or bracelet page.
The size guide and free resizing are shown plainly, not buried in a policy page: "Free resizing within 30 days".
Size, not price, is the number one reason a jewellery basket is abandoned. Removing the anxiety converts hesitation into an order without discounting a single riyal.
A ring page → "Free resizing for 30 days" beside the buy button, not in the policies.
The order is a gift, or falls in an occasion season.
The gift box and a handwritten card are offered as one option, not two. The moment of opening is part of the product in this sector.
Someone spending three thousand on a necklace will not hesitate over a hundred for packaging that fits - but they will not go looking for it. Offering it at the right moment is near-pure margin.
A necklace as a gift → a velvet box and a handwritten card at 120 SAR, as one option.
Caring for the piece after the purchase
The customer buys a silver or stone-set piece.
Care tools are presented as instructions: "Silver tarnishes; a polishing cloth brings it back". Information first, product second.
A piece that dulls after two months becomes a complaint about the store rather than a lesson in care. Selling the care kit protects the piece's reputation.
A silver bracelet → "A polishing cloth, 45 SAR", with one line on why it tarnishes.
Silver tarnishes; polishing brings it back
An occasion on which the customer bought before is approaching.
A reminder with enough lead time for shipping and resizing: "Your anniversary is in two weeks". Late buying is impossible in jewellery, so timing is the service.
Someone who bought for an annual occasion will buy again, and the store that reminds them before the shop next door wins the whole order.
Bought on 12 March last year → a reminder on 26 February with similar pieces.
Two weeks out - time to ship and resize
A necklace from the same collection
Trading up on a difference you can see
The customer is comparing two close pieces.
The difference is explained in what can be seen rather than in jargon: "Half a carat bigger, 600 SAR apart", not "VS1 clarity instead of SI2".
Quality jargon means nothing to a non-specialist and makes them postpone. Translating it into a visible difference is what closes.
A 4,200 ring → "Same design, larger stone, +600", with a true-size comparison image.

Livestock is sharply seasonal and logistically hard: most of the year's demand falls in a handful of days, the product is alive and cannot be stocked, and delivery is tied to an appointment rather than a shipment. And the buyer cares about two things before price: that the animal is as described, and that it arrives exactly on time. Every moment below serves one of those two.
Cutting and preparation with the order
Preparation options are laid out plainly: cutting, mincing, portioned vacuum packing, splitting across addresses. All priced services rather than assumptions.
Preparation is the real margin here, because the animal's own price is broadly known to everyone. It also saves the customer an entire day.
A Naimi sheep → "Cutting 80, mincing a quarter 40, portioned packing 60".
Booking before the season, not during it
An Eid, aqiqah or banquet season approaches.
Early booking is offered with a locked price and a guaranteed slot. Whoever books on the day pays more and may find nothing.
Capacity in season is genuinely finite. Early booking spreads demand across days instead of hours, which is the difference between a good season and a chaotic one.

Upgrade the size by the difference, not the price
The guest picks a medium latte and opens the item sheet.
The larger size appears with the difference alone: "Large +3 SAR", never "Large 22 SAR". A difference is a small number compared against the cup; a full price is compared against the budget.
Size upgrades carry some of the highest margin in a cafe, because the added cost is milk and a cup. It is also the easiest yes on the menu: it adds no item and no waiting time.
Medium latte 19 SAR → large for 3 SAR more. Same cup, same wait.
The top three add-ons in this branch
The guest opens an item that has paid modifiers.
Instead of a twenty-option modifier list, three chips only: the most-ordered with this item in this branch specifically. Choosing from three is a decision; choosing from twenty is a burden.
Modifiers are almost pure margin. Ranking by branch rather than by chain matters: the campus branch orders an extra shot, the family branch orders cream.
Latte → extra shot +4 SAR, almond milk, hazelnut. Three chips, one tap.
Turn the item into a meal in one tap
The guest adds a burger with no side and no drink.
A single toggle: "Make it a meal +9 SAR". It reaches the POS as one combo rather than three loose items, so the kitchen reads it right and the bill prints right.
A guest ordering a lone burger will usually buy a drink anyway. The meal captures that purchase before they leave rather than losing it.
Burger 32 SAR → meal at 41 SAR (fries and a drink for 9).
Ordered with it, here and now
The guest opens their cart before submitting.
One card with one item: what is actually ordered alongside what is in the cart, in this branch and this daypart. If there is already a drink in the order, no second drink is suggested.

What goes with what in the morning is not what goes with it at night. A croissant rides with coffee at eight; cake rides with it at nine in the evening. The same suggestion at the wrong hour gets declined.
Regular shawarma 18 SAR → "ordered with it": mini kunafa 15 SAR.
Complete the offer: one item short
The cart holds two of the three items in a defined bundle.
The offer is not advertised up front but at the edge of it: "One orange juice away from the breakfast bundle, 8 SAR off". It names the missing item exactly, so the guest does not go hunting.
An offer shown up front is a discount on something already being bought. An offer shown one item short adds that item. The difference between the two is the difference between a cost and a margin.
Hot coffee + butter croissant in the cart → "Add an orange juice at 14 and save 8".
"Any 3 pastries for 30 SAR" - without naming which. The guest picks the third themselves, so it reads as a choice rather than a sell.
An any-N bundle moves slow stock without visibly discounting it, and keeps the list price intact for anyone buying a single item.
Zaatar croissant 12 + blueberry muffin 12 + cheese danish 13 = 37 → 30 SAR.
The cart ladder: how far to the next tier
The cart total sits close to a higher discount tier.
A progress bar states the gap in riyals, with exactly two items that close it - fast to prepare, not retail, and sorted by smallest overshoot rather than highest price.
Sorting by smallest overshoot rather than highest price is the difference between helping and squeezing. A guest 7 SAR short is not offered a 42 SAR item.
Cart at 43 SAR, the 50 tier gives 5% → "7 SAR to go". It suggests a 12 SAR croissant, not a 42 SAR cookie box.
Actually costs you: the price after the offer kicks in
Adding an item would push the cart into a higher tier.

Two prices show: the list price, and under it "actually costs you 13.10" - because adding it unlocked a discount on the whole order. The figure is computed, not marketing: it is what you pay with the item minus what you pay without it.
This is the most honest argument on the page, and it is also what revenue attribution is measured against. It only ever shows when it is genuinely lower than the list price.
Cheesecake 18 SAR on a 62 SAR cart → actually 13.10, because the order crossed the 5% tier.
Say to the table: a ready sentence, not training
The waiter has entered the items and not yet sent to the kitchen.
A card with the spoken sentence verbatim, and three buttons: added / declined / didn't offer. The third matters: it separates a waiter who tried and failed from one who never tried.
Upselling in restaurants is normally trained in a session that is forgotten in a week. A ready sentence at the moment replaces the training, and the measurement shows who uses it.
"The shawarma goes with a mini kunafa for fifteen - want me to add it?" → three outcome buttons.

Twenty minutes have passed since the mains went to the kitchen.

The table flips to "dessert time" in the waiter's list, with a suggestion built from what that table actually ordered. Offering dessert with the first order gets declined; offering it after the food gets accepted.
Dessert is the highest-margin line on a restaurant menu and the most forgotten one. Timing alone is the difference, and nobody on the floor has time to watch twenty tables by the clock.
A table ordered grills at 7:40 → 8:00 alert: "Kunafa and Arabic coffee for the table?"

The order closed on the POS and preparation started.

One message to the guest's phone during the wait: "Add this before it's ready" - and a second order is created, linked to the first. It never touches the cashier screen or delays the queue behind them.
The wait is dead time the guest already spends on their phone, and it is the only window where a suggestion competes with nothing.
Burger ordered 8:02 → 8:03 message: "Fresh cookies just came out, 8 SAR?"

The order is ready and it contained coffee.
One suggestion that never repeats: "Liked our coffee? A 250g bag of beans". It appears after the preparation window closes, not before - before it, the guest has not tasted anything yet.
Selling beans carries more margin than a cup and a longer tail, but it needs proof by taste. Offering it with the order gets ahead of the proof.
A Spanish latte in the order → after it is ready: "The same beans, 250g bag".

The usual order in one tap, and beside it one item they have never ordered. The usual saves them a minute; the new item is what widens what they order.
A repeat customer orders the same thing because it is easier, not because it is better. One new item per visit lifts their lifetime basket without reading as a sell.

How Does AI Learn About Your Customers?

The AI in Ziadah is not just a set of fixed programming rules — it is a system that continuously learns and evolves based on your store's unique data. Understanding how it works helps you use it more intelligently.

During every visit to your store, the system quietly tracks: What did the customer view? What did they add to the cart? What did they ultimately buy? What did they ignore? This data is stored in a completely anonymous manner.

The system looks for common patterns: "Customers who bought A usually also bought B." This is called Collaborative Filtering. The more data there is, the more precise and personalized patterns the system discovers.
When a new customer visits your store, the system compares their current behavior with millions of stored patterns, then selects the most likely successful recommendation in seconds.
After every recommendation, the system learns from the result: Did the customer click? Did they buy? If not, what did they do instead? This feedback makes the system smarter over time.

CTR (Click-Through Rate): the percentage of people who clicked your link/ad out of all who saw it (for example, 50 clicks out of 1000 views = 5%).
AOV (Average Order Value): average amount spent per order, calculated as total sales divided by number of orders.
Basket AOV (Average Basket Value): average value of the full basket after add-ons/bundles are added in the same session; this reflects recommendation impact on final basket value.
Attachment Rate: the percentage of orders that include an add-on item with the main product.
CVR (Conversion Rate): the percentage of visits/clicks that complete the target action such as purchase or form submission.
Profit Margin: the percentage of profit remaining after subtracting costs from sales.
Retention Rate: the share of customers who came back and bought again within a period, rather than buying once and disappearing.
Cart Rescue: the share of abandoned carts whose owners came back and completed the order after a well-timed reminder or suggestion.
Recurring Conversion: the share of one-off donors who moved to a recurring monthly gift - the number a charity's economics turn on.
Average Gift: the average value of a single donation. It is the charity equivalent of average order value, but the unit is a gift rather than an order.

This page explains how a merchant can request deletion of their account and store data from Ziadah, what gets deleted, and how long it takes. These instructions are designed to satisfy the user-data-deletion requirements of Meta, Snapchat, Google, and TikTok, as well as the Zid, Salla and Shopify marketplaces and Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL).
1. Uninstall the app from your store

From your Zid, Salla or Shopify dashboard, open Apps and remove the Ziadah app. Uninstalling triggers an automatic webhook, at which point we begin deleting the access tokens and store data linked to the app.
Sign in to the Ziadah dashboard and go to Settings → Account → Delete account & data, then follow the confirmation steps. This removes your account, store data, and reports.

A request covers: merchant account data (name and email), store data imported via the Zid, Salla and Shopify APIs (products and orders), OAuth access tokens, recommendation-interaction data, and the reports and analytics linked to your account.

To protect your account, we may ask you to confirm ownership of the store (for example, from the registered email address or from within the dashboard) before we delete anything, so that unauthorized requests are prevented.
We acknowledge your request within 72 business hours and complete deletion within a maximum of 30 days. Access tokens are deleted immediately on uninstall.

We may keep a minimum set of records (such as invoices and transaction logs) for the period required by law for accounting or legal purposes, and we may keep aggregated, anonymized data that cannot be linked to you or your store. Everything else is permanently deleted.

If you connect your advertising accounts, or we use Meta, Snapchat, Google, or TikTok to process any data on your behalf, fulfilling a deletion request includes stopping any transfer of your data to those platforms and deleting what we hold. This page serves as the approved Data Deletion Instructions URL that those platforms review when approving our app.
